utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom and to those who are following our procedure. Due to technical problems in Courtroom III we are, again, in Courtroom II now. I would like to raise two matters. Mr. Tolimir, Mr. Gajic, you have received a confidential motion, I think it was confidential because of medical information contained in it, for leave to add Witness Dumanjic to it's witness list. It's not a protected witness. We can expect the B/C/S translation to be filed by the end of today or tomorrow, and I would like to invite the Defence, if possible, to respond to that orally in the course of this week, perhaps on Thursday, because we are now really approaching the end of the Prosecution case and, therefore, we should speed up the best possible way. Mr. Gajic, would that be possible for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as you know so far this Defence has been efficient and our written reply is already prepared. It just needs to go through a minor revision. I believe it will be filed tomorrow or the day after tomorrow at the latest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you now referring to the two 92 quater submissions of the Prosecution or to this motion to add a witness to the witness list, Mr. Gajic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The submission concerning the addition of a new witness to the schedule, and we will probably file a combined submission responding to all the three motions of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. That will speed up the remainder of the Prosecution case, for sure. There is another matter I would like to raise. Early in this trial, I indicated that we will probably hold a housekeeping session at the end of the Prosecution case. I am not sure which matters could be discussed in such a housekeeping session. I would kindly ask the parties if they have some matters to discuss during a housekeeping session, and if so, what kind of matters the parties would like to put on the agenda. If there is no need for that, then we should refrain from having such a housekeeping session. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. And I -- of course, we will discuss that, Mr. Gajic and myself, but as you know we communicate so often with each other and with the Court, I can't think of anything off the top of my head, but we'll discuss it and see. There is probably -- there may be something out there, but right now I can't think of anything, but we will get together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is a rare opportunity when I share Mr. McCloskey's opinion. There are no issues to raise at such a housekeeping session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I am astonished that you say this is a rare opportunity. My experience is different, on procedural matters there is a very good relation between the parties and a good co-operation. We appreciate that. Thank you for that. I would kindly ask the Defence about the estimation of time to be used between the next two witnesses, Michael Hedley and Jan de Koeijer. Are you able to provide us with your estimate for cross-examination. At least I didn't receive any indication. I was informed by the Registrar that we, indeed, received your estimation, one and a half hours for both of the witnesses. Thank you. The next witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Hedley. Welcome to this trial and to the courtroom. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down and make yourself comfortable. Mr. Elderkin, for the Prosecution, has questions for you. You have the floor, Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And good afternoon to you, Your Honours, and to everyone else in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you, Mr. Hedley.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: As I mentioned when we had the chance to meet yesterday, since we are both speaking the same language and the proceedings are being interpreted, we should both try and go slowly. And the best way to allow the interpreters to keep up is to leave a pause after I ask a question before you start answering, and I will try to leave a pause after your answer before I carry on.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Also I know you brought some papers in with you this afternoon, could you just tell us what those papers are?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: This is a copy of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And could you please move a little bit further toward the microphones. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How is that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a copy of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: That's fine, it's just so that everyone in the Court knows what you've brought in. I should ask, first, for the record, that you say your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: My name is Michael John Hedley.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak into the microphone? He can be barely heard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Michael John Hedley.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And what is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: British.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think there is a technical problem with the microphones. Perhaps the Court Usher -- it's hardly to be heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it's coming from this microphone here, which I'm about to unplug and replace with the original one. So if you give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Silence, which I think is a good thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please, try it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: So I think we have on the record, sir, your name. If you could repeat, please, your nationality?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: British.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: My current occupation is that of a regional property manager for a development company in the UK.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: When did you start that work?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: 2002, after I left as a contractor with ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And so what was your previous career?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: I am a retired police officer. I retired from the police service in the UK in 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And starting from when you first joined the police service, can you talk us through briefly that career in the police in Britain.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: It was a long time ago. Yes, I'll try. I joined the police service in 1970 as a uniformed police officer in a county known as Teesside in northern England.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I think we are still picking you up. That's fine if you carry on.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's just a change in the -- yes, I joined in 1970 in the Teesside in the north of England. I served in that constabulary for five years, and I transferred to Gloucestershire constabulary which in the southwest of England. In 1975, I was a uniformed police officer, I served so until 1980, when I took an interest in scenes of crime work, took an attachment with the scenes of crime department of the Gloucestershire constabulary. I took an initial training source at the national scientific aides' college in the UK. I was subsequently accepted within the department, and carried on as a scenes of crime officer for a number of years until, I think, 1996. During that period, within scenes of crime, obviously, I started off at the bottom dealing with the most minor crimes such as theft of motor vehicles, minor assaults, then went on to investigation of burglary, more serious crimes of rape, sexual assault, up to crimes of attempted murder and murder. Obviously, I was mentored throughout the early service, and then became a senior examiner in my own right later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What was the nature of the training that you received at the national college that you attended to qualify as a scene of crime officer?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: We were taught all aspects of crime scene investigation, from finger-print retrieval through to collection of forensic exhibits, packaging, preservation, for later submission to the forensic science laboratories. We were also trained in photography and technical photography of particular items found, evidential items found or collected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Perhaps by way of example, can you talk us through what a scene of crime officer does on any given case, bearing in mind you're the first such professional that we have heard give evidence in this trial?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: Perhaps I could describe the approach towards a burglary scene. Obviously uniformed department would be called to the burglary first, and then if the uniformed officers thought that there was a scene to examine, they would request attendance of a scenes of crime officer. I would attend, obviously approach the scene with a view to collecting evidence on the same approach that perhaps the burglar would have taken. I would then look at the point of entry, in particular look at any tool-marks which were used to force entry. I would also look for traces of fibres, perhaps even if the offender was injured, traces of blood. At that point, if I haven't found any of these particular articles of evidence, I would take photographs. I would take photographs with scales attached to them to -- in case of a subsequent inquiry for forensic examination. I would collect blood samples by means of a swab. I would clearly mark the swab package to indicate the area -- the address in which it was recovered. In the case of tool-marks, which would obviously be in a fixed window frame which couldn't be removed, I would probably use a casting material to cast the impression made by the tool. Again, that's -- once the cast had set, I would remove the cast and probably store it in a crush-proof box so it couldn't be damaged, clearly mark it up for subsequent submission for forensic science laboratory. Once the physical -- again, things like fibres, fibres might perhaps be adherent to a point of entry, on a jagged piece of wood, say, for example, in which case I would use a tape method of placing tape over the fibre, lifting the fibre, and then attaching that to a celluloid sheet. Again I would write on the sheet, clearly marking the address of the property, the precise location where it was found in relation to the point of entry. Again, I would clearly mark the time and date of retrieval. Then, a finger-print examination would take place around that point of entry, in particular looking at a place of entry where a person might have pulled themselves, which is always a favourite of raising finger-prints. That would be done with how aluminum powder and soft brush. Sometimes there would be a finger-print in blood where you could actually see the finger-print in which case you would have to take a photograph of the finger-print.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedley, may I ask you to slow down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You are speaking very fast, and you must bear in mind that we have interpreters who have to interpret everything which you are saying into French and B/C/S and it's better to slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lost my train now. There are -- obviously, an examination would then carry on inside the property. In particular, looking for, perhaps, foot-prints which obviously would have also taken place outside, footprints on windowsills.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If I may interrupt there. I think you have given us a very clear flavor of the detail with which a task is approached. You've described a number of examples of the specific kinds of evidence in a burglary situation you might be looking for and the detailed way in which you would record and then store that evidence. Were you following set protocols in your approach to this, or does a scene of crime officer develop their own specific methods of work?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: No, there is a --

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And if you could leave a pause again, just for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: The word "protocol" is a word, it's attached, I think, with something I found with the ICTY in the sites. But there was a set method which we were taught during our basic training, and particularly it was that of a collect -- method of collection of the evidence and method of preservation of the evidence, and the correct storage of the evidence. And then a chain of custody from myself to whoever else the investigating officer decided to submit the sample to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And just to get back to the end of your career with the British police, can you tell us what was your last employment with the police and then when did you retire from the police?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: In 1996, I was offered a position of criminal intelligence officer within the Gloucestershire crime intelligence unit. I served there for four years until my retirement in 6th of January, 2000. I took a couple of months off and approached ICTY with a view to employment in the exhumation scheme.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And you managed to obtain employment with the ICTY. Can you tell us what terms you were employed and what position you were employed --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: I was --

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And again just pause for a moment, first, please.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: I was employed as a scene of crime officer, as a contractor, as ICTY working under Professor Richard Wright.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I see in the transcript it says you were employed as a senior crime. I think I heard scene of crime officer.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: Scene of crime officer is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And this employment as ICTY scene of crime officer started in 2000. Where did you carry out your work for the ICTY in the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: During 2000, we commenced in Croatia, at the site of -- sorry, I can't remember the name of the site. We came across to Sanski Most and worked at Prijedor cemetery, a site called Redak which was a stoneworks. Then we came across to Visoko [Realtime transcript read in error "Bisko"] and worked on sites within the Srebrenica inquiry. I worked at Lazete I and II, Glogova 1, and I was requested to carry out an examination at Kravica warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And when did you leave the ICTY or leave your employment for the ICTY, I should say?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: At the end of 2000 I left the Srebrenica team, Richard Wright's team, and then commenced the following year, and worked a season, a couple of months, with Jose Pablo Baraybar's team, and then requested I moved to the monitoring team, where I worked with Jon Sterenburg for the remainder of the season at Cancari Road and Liplje sites, and Ravnice sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can I just pick up one word that appears, if you look at the live transcript. At page 10, line 4, it refers to a place called "Bisko"?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Now, focussing on your Srebrenica-related work, you've mentioned your work at Lazete 1 and 2 sites, Glogova 1, Kravica, and then the following year also at Ravnice, and I think you mentioned Liplje, although it doesn't appear on the LiveNote at the moment. Does that cover all the sites for which you worked in relation to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, that includes them all, yes. I don't know the numbers of the Liplje sites or the Cancari road, but I think we did four or five sites, those locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And what function did you perform at the different sites? Again, just in relation to the Srebrenica sites.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: Well, in 2000, I was senior scene of crime officer on site. I had assistants, data entry assistance who also assistant SOCO. Later on in the season, much later on in the season, we had two Dutch scene of crime officers joined us at Glogova 1, and -- apologies, going back to Lazete, we also had a South African SOCO that assisted us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: How did you work as a scene of crime officer at these Srebrenica related sites compare to your experience as scene of crime officer during your police service back in Britain?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: Well, the intensity on site was obviously much greater than the more relaxed work carried out on domestic scene of crime in an urban police force. Generally speaking, the principles were basically the same, the volume of work was just that much greater.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can you describe, perhaps by, again, way of example for any of the Srebrenica sites where you worked, what other professionals were present and working at those sites. So you mentioned yourself as the senior scene of crime officer and also assistant scene of crime officers. Who else would have been present at a typical site and what would their functions have been?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: Well, obviously there was the senior archeologist, and in the case of 2000, it was Professor Wright, with one break where Fredy Peccerelli took over at Lazete. Also on site were several other senior archeologists, and experienced anthropologists. We had one archeologist who was also the total operator, the electronic theodolite operator who used the map the sites. We obviously had the support staff, who comprised of three or four chaps who generally looked after these sites and our amenities. There were drivers. We had a photographer who was an archaeological photographer. I think I have covered it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Where would you stay during the course of your work on these sites?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: We were billeted -- in respect of Srebrenica, we were billeted at Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness kindly speak closer to the microphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Glogova 1 as one of the sites that you worked on in 2000 in relation to Srebrenica, can you tell us about your work on that site? Again, a brief summary as far as you remember when you arrived there, what work was being carried out.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: To my recollection when we first arrived, I think it was postponed and we actually went -- I believe we started Rovici [phoen]. I can't quite remember. But basically my duties would have been that of opening up an evidence log and issuing numbers to particular items of evidence that were uncovered, and eventually taking possession of those items, securely packaging them, storing them for later handover to the mortuary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you remember the site well enough to give us a brief description of the site or its surroundings?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. It was a large site, just at the bottom of a valley. It was close to the main road between Bratunac and Konjevic Polje. The site itself was flat. It was a large site. It was, I think, four or five houses around the site. Probably three of them had been completely demolished, they had been blown up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And perhaps just for orientation, if we could have Exhibit P104 on the screen, and at page 8, I think, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, I am just bringing up what I hope is a simplified map just so we can see the locations that you've just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And as I say, can we have page 8, I think, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, looking now at the map on the screen, you could see a red dot around the -- just above the centre of the map marked with Kravica, and then to the right-hand side of the screen Bratunac, and then down towards the bottom, Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: That's correct. Could I -- I've checked it on the -- my monitor on the vehicle I was driving. Kravica is about 8 kilometres from Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And we can see Glogova on this map, then, on the road running -- starting at Konjevic Polje, going past Sandici, Kravica, then Glogova, and then finally to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And we --

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I don't need to have the map anymore for the following question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: But do you recall if any ICTY investigators were involved during the course of the excavations at Glogova 1?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Dean Manning was obviously on-site quite often, Bruce Bursik was on site, Jean Gagnon was on site, and a Finnish investigator called Kai, as I remember. I can't remember his surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can we have Exhibit P873 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, while this is loading up, it's going to be the report that Professor Richard Wright wrote about the Glogova 1 excavations and exhumations work in 2000. First, have you ever seen this report before, actually?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I have. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could we go, please, to page 3 in e-court. I think the B/C/S will be the same. And let us read a little bit from the summary findings, but they tell us how the work at Glogova 1 was carried out in September and October 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And about halfway down it reads: "Several objects considered to be from the Kravica warehouse were found in the graves and Mr. Michael Hedley is writing a separate report on the connection between the warehouse and Glogova 1." We will come to your report in a minute, but first I want to ask you about the features of the Glogova exhumations that led Professor Wright and the team to believe that there might be a connection with the Kravica site. Can you tell us what sort of features those were. What gave this sort of indication?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: Initially, it was obvious that certain elements were being uncovered which included pieces of concrete, painted concrete, in the process of removing the upper spoil from the grave. There was a couple of metal doors which were scraped off the surfaces of A and B sections. And also was found a painted metal girder. But as we got into the grave, as I say, these concrete pieces were significant, because it was known, I believe, that in order to remove the bodies from the Kravica warehouse they had to break open the front of the warehouse in order to get a digger in to the facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: The last piece of information you mentioned that it was known that they had to break in the front of the warehouse to get a digger to remove the bodies. Do you recall where you learnt that information and about what period of time are we talking about when you say that the bodies were removed from the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: Where the information had come from, it was obviously just part of a briefing. Whether that came from Professor Wright, himself, or one of the investigators, I can't quite recall, but we were aware of what we were probably going to find.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And when you say that "they had to break in the front of the warehouse," who are you referring to by "they" and when are these people breaking down the front of the warehouse, according to your information?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: Well, we assumed it was the perpetrators or those people employed by the perpetrators to remove the bodies and take them for burial, so we would assume the Bosnian VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And in what kind of time-period would that have happened?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: That would have been in July 1995. I can't remember the dates exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Now, could we go back to the exhibit we've just had on screen and to page 17 in e-court, please. And actually one page prior to that, please, in English. So page 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I will carry on speaking while if B/C/S comes up. This page has a heading on it: "Properties of graves and bodies." And then some details are listed beneath that, including a list of graves with different letters. Can you tell us if you recall whether there were several different graves at the Glogova site? Because it appears from this table that there are different designations for different graves?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: Yeah, these designations were obviously given by Professor Wright in his capacity as the chief archeologist. As regards the number of bodies found, that was not my job to count bodies at all. But, quite rightly, in my report I do mention the difference between the excavation and the graves, but in my report I concentrate on the artefacts, in particular, the concrete and the girders that were found within those graves -- within particular graves that would have connected them to Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And could we go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And I won't be asking you in detail about the bodies. I understand that your focus was on the artefacts. I would just like to look at one more paragraph underneath the properties of graves and bodies section. Which is, if we look at the top of this page, and the third paragraph down starting: "In the light ..." And it reads: "In the light of this unusual fragmentation of bodies that are in situ, I consider it significant that Glogova 1 is the only primary site where I have found remains of explosive devices in the form of grenades and shrapnel." First of all, sir, do you remember whether such items were recovered at the Glogova site?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: I can't remember the detail of the log, but I would have to look at the log to remember those particular items.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And then if we could move on to e-court page 19, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And this page is where Professor Wright lists under the heading of "Possible connections with the Kravica warehouse," a number of points of linkage. Perhaps we could scroll down to see the indented points. Sir, looking down this list and the kind of items listed here, so fragments of reinforced cement panel, fragments of cement fins, polystyrene foam, lumps of cut grass, pieces of metal door frame, we've already heard you mention, panels of metal for covering a door, some rolled steel joists, and finally, motor vehicle parts. To the best of your recollection, are these the sorts of things that were being found in the Glogova exhumations?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: Yeah, just one point. Professor Wright mentions "rolled steel joists." I would call them open box section girders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I would certainly defer to your experience, now, given your current profession in the construction industry. If we could go one page further from that. As you can see at the top it refers to you: "Mr. Michael Hedley, scene of crime officer at Glogova 1 is writing a detailed report on items from Glogova 1 and their comparison with the Kravica warehouse." Could you tell us how it came about that you were asked to write the report? Do you remember who tasked you and what the instructions were that you received?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: It was obviously following discussions between Professor Wright, the investigator -- investigators, and myself, as to whether, A, I was proficient in collecting those samples and able and willing to provide a report for the Court to -- in an attempt to create that connection between the two sites -- a forensic connection between the two sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Before we get into the report in detail, I would like to go to a couple more references in Professor Wright's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: First of all, at e-court in page 38. If we could please, first of all, zoom in to better see the photograph at the top of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: In you're able, sir, can you describe to us what kind of scene we're seeing here and how this relates to the question of artefacts from Kravica being found in the Glogova grave?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: What we see is, as you say, it's a grave, you can see bodies and body parts, you can also see the girder to which I earlier referred to. We have four archeologists, Jon Sterenburg [Realtime transcript read in error "Stellenburg"], Jean Marie [phoen], Gina Hart, and I can't recollect the name of the male archeologists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the name slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jean Marie, on the left. On the right is Gina Hart, and behind, with the pad, is Jon Sterenburg. And I can't quite recollect the name of the male archeologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And can we scroll down now to see the images below that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just looking at the screen, it's actually Sterenberg, not Stellenberg. S-t-e-r-e-n-b-e-r-g.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And what was the first name. This is also missing in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Jean Marie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Okay. If the names are cleared up, then. If we can look back at the images, perhaps you can tell us what we are seeing, are these pictures all taken at Glogova or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: Photo 56665_11a, is the doorway of Kravica warehouse as we found it when we arrived in September 2000. Photo 56759_10a shows part of a door which I will refer to in my report in amongst, as you see, body parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And if we could just scroll down to see that image just beneath.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: I am afraid I can't quite make that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If you take a moment, sir, also to perhaps read the text underneath. And if we could zoom slightly out, in fact, to read the width of the text beneath the picture. According to the footnote headed figure 14, sir, it refers to?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: Of course, that's polystyrene, it's not a particularly good photograph, but it's -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And could we go to the next page in e-court as well, please. And zooming in at the top, please.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: That looks like a hydraulic jack.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Would that have come from the Glogova grave?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: That was in Glogova, yes, that's marked as 146, which would have been an artefact.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness kindly speak louder. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. Yes, it's a hydraulic jack, the photograph is marked GL01 146, which would be an artefact recorded in the evidence log.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could we scroll down to the second image please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, a wheel off a vehicle, next to some clothing. To the left I can see some metal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And the final image beneath that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And again, if necessary, there is a written description beneath there.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I see body, body parts, clothing, and grass beneath the body or the body part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you know if the presence of the cut grass had any significance in terms of establishing a connection with Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: I personally didn't collect any samples from Kravica warehouse which could have, to my recollection, could have been compared with that but Richard Wright -- Professor Wright obviously saw significance in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Okay. Now we will turn to your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And that is at 65 ter number 7519, please. I understand, Your Honours, for your information, this is not technically on the 65 ter list, but given its been the basis of our request to call Mr. Hedley for some considerable time, I don't think there is anything controversial about requesting its addition to the 65 ter list at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, my usual question: Are you fine with adding this document to the 65 ter exhibit list?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am fine with that. And it has been common practice for the Prosecutor to add documents in this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Leave is granted, Mr. Elderkin. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And if we could look quickly -- I think we will start with the cover of your report, sir, since it's the first time we have had a chance to see it. This, I take it, is the end product of the investigation you carried out. When did you write the report and can you give us a brief description of what work you did in order to produce the report?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: I left Bosnia I think it was in November of 2001. Obviously, I took Christmas break, and I commenced my report, I think, in January, the first draft. I gathered up all the information I could that I was allowed to take with me from Bosnia and commenced writing the report which was the early stage of what you see today. We took -- I took a month out on holiday with my wife, came back in probably March, and I finished the report at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And if we can go to the next page in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And without needing to repeat what's written there, can you give us a brief overview of the structure of the report and then of the conclusions that you arrived at?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: Well, for clarity, I broke up the report into two halves. It makes it easier to read, and understand, and compare. And you want my final conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Yeah, if you could put the conclusions in context of the question that you were asked, which I understand was to determine what might be the links between Kravica warehouse and the Glogova grave?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: That's right. Yes, it's a collection describing what I saw at Glogova 1 and the exhibits, the artefacts, control samples, that I collected from Kravica warehouse, and comparing them within the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And could we go please to e-court page 20 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, for your information that's your own internal numbering, page 19. And there, I think, the report states the conclusions, but can you perhaps talk us through those just to give us a direct view of what you state there?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: As I say, all the exhibits that were recovered under the control samples were collected with a view to comparison, where appropriate, where a camera was available, photographs were taken with a scale adjacent for future reference or for future forensic examination. I prepared a list of all the relevant items listed by description and location together with this suggested forensic or investigative comparison with control samples taken from the warehouse, from Kravica warehouse. I also noted at this point that there was a possibility of contamination from the houses I described earlier that had been blown up on the Glogova site, I think three of them had been blown up, and one of those houses that I searched I found on the floor were blue tiles, and the blue tiles were similar in appearance, not only in colour, but also on the reverse of the tile indicating they were probably the same manufacturer. I would say this contamination was only in relation to the tile. We also found in that house insulating material similar to polystyrene insulate material which wasn't similar to that that I recovered as a control sample from the Kravica warehouse or that we were finding within Glogova 1 grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, what conclusion did you arrive at if you had to summarise in a sentence or two in terms of identifying links between Kravica and Glogova?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: Well, as I said in my report, the action of enlarging the doorway at the Kravica warehouse in order to gain that vehicle access would have resulted in the component parts of that doorway being pushed inside of the building and falling amongst the bodies of the victims that lay inside. Therefore, it would have been inevitable of a bucket vehicle to have scooped up those bodies, they would have also scooped up the demolished doorway. These together would have been conveyed to the burial place. And, as we suspected, if Glogova 1 was the burial place, you must consider that there is substantial evidence that those men killed in the Kravica warehouse in July 1995 were amongst the same men whose remains were recovered from Glogova 1 in September and October 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I might go into some more detail about the specific linkages and hopefully put some images on the screen, but in order to keep track of things I would ask at this stage for the report to be admitted as an exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7519 shall be assigned Exhibit P2591. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could we please have exhibit P94 on the screen and at page 97 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And sir, for your information, this is a photographic exhibit that I was able to show you briefly yesterday which contains a series of different photographs around the Kravica area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we move to that part of your examination, Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I am very interested, intrigued, by your conclusion concerning the connection between the mass grave of Glogova and the Kravica warehouse. We have just seen on one of the photos that there was some sort of vehicle, and a metal object that looked like a shock absorber, and some plants among the bodies. You just said that the vehicle pieces originated from Kravica warehouse. Do you have any explanation for those plants? Do you have any evidence to support that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally can't give any evidence regarding the plants found beneath the body, but I didn't go into detail to describe - which I probably should have done - the fact that the breaking open of the doorway of the Kravica warehouse would have resulted in much of the masonry surrounding the original doorway being broken away and falling on top of the bodies. This included a lot of concrete, a lot of insulating material, and of course it also included the reddish maroon fins which were either decorative on the front of the warehouse or had the functional purpose of strengthening the front of the warehouse. Now, these were significant in the fact that they were painted a particular colour and we were we are finding the same pieces within the Glogova 1 grave painted that same colour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. But concerning the pieces of vehicles and the plants found around the bodies, no other explanation has been found; is that the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understood that from our original briefing when we were told what we could expect to find within the warehouse -- sorry, within the graves that had been taken from the warehouse, the witness had mentioned that prior to the victims being detained within warehouse, there had been vehicle parts within that warehouse. So those would have been there before the victims arrived. Presumably, they were removed with the victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, that's it. Now I understand. There are witnesses who claimed that there were parts of vehicles inside the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I understand it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If I could return to the exhibit we were bringing up in e-court, and ask to go to page 97.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I will ask you a number of questions about the work at the Kravica site, but to start with and give us some context, can you tell us what we are seeing in these images here?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: We are seeing the north aspect of the Kravica warehouse, and outlined in red is the area where I undertook my examination. The original -- the first visit to Kravica warehouse describes recovery of shell cases and some skull fragments. That search was carried out in front of the small red box on the grassed area in front of the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If I could ask you to talk to us about a couple of features on the images. First of all, in the superimposed image, the winter scene where we see snow on the ground, there is a very large opening in the warehouse, within the red box. Does that correspond with how the warehouse looked when you saw the warehouse or, if not, what were the differences?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: The difference to the doorway that we saw in September 2000 is the doorway then had a new lintel in it and there was some reconstruction above that lintel to close off the doorway to the roof level.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And perhaps we could zoom in to the bottom right of the image which I think will show the appearance as you describe. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: That's right. And painted at the front. What's also interesting, to the right of that box it shows a smaller building which was -- contained -- was presumably a boiler house and that's where I recovered a paint tin which contained paint which was, to the naked eye, similar to the paint colour on the artefacts found at the Glogova 1 site.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: We may see this better in a later image, but you have mentioned the concrete fins on the building, and we can see here a number of pairs of vertical lines along the white facade of the building. Are those the concrete fins that you have been talking about?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: Yeah, those are the fins as I described them. You see, they are uniformly spaced. They fit in with the pre-cast concrete slabs which were interlocked together. So everything would just fit really neatly together. It -- if I can later refer to my computer-generated reconstruction of the door using the dimensions of the door as we knew them and dimensions and the distance between the interlocking fins, and also the witness marks which we discovered at the doorway which showed an open box section and showed the actual position of the actual doorway.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And do I understand that you're referring to the page marked as appendix 2 in your report, sir? If you just give us a reference so we can find that later?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, appendix 2. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did your investigation at the Kravica warehouse involve also going inside the building, or did you just perform your work outside?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: No, obviously we had to go inside. As I recall inside, there was -- there was some seed grain in there, which was infested with vermin. When we first went in, there was -- mice scurried all over. To one side, there was some wooden window frames but they were undamaged and unglazed as I recall. To the back of the warehouse, halfway up the wall were some wooden window frames but again there was no encasements in them. To the left of the warehouse there was what appeared to be the witness marks, as I described the witness marks, it's the bonding marks where there was an internal room within the building, small room. There were blue tiles to the base of the wall of that small room, I suspect it was probably a kitchen or a washroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If we could go to page 105 in e-court. And if you could comment on that image once it comes up, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can clearly see where that room was placed. It was -- it was roofed -- it was the vertical and horizontal bonding marks of the structure that was attached to it. And you can also see in that photograph quite clearly the blue tiles at the base of the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Was this particular area of the warehouse of any relevance in relation to your investigation when you were seeking to find connections with the Glogova 1 site?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: In respect of -- we took control samples of the blue tile and we -- also beneath the debris you see on the floor there was vinyl tile as well, and I took control samples of the vinyl tile for comparison.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can we now see, please, page 108 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And these photographs, I take it, are all part of the report of Mr. Hedley, P2591; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. At the moment we are looking at the photo book used with Jean-Rene Ruez. It's Exhibit P94, obviously already admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, this is another interior shot of the warehouse. Does the condition seen in this image reflect how you saw the warehouse or, if not, how did it differ when you saw it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: Yeah, that's pretty much the same. The walls pockmarked with bullets. There was evidence that a fire had taken place within the warehouse, as you can see, by the blackening of the walls and ceiling.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If we could go back, please, to Mr. Hedley's report which has just been assigned P2591. And go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If you want to stay with this photograph for a moment, Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Just now you have said there was evidence that a fire had taken place within the warehouse. Can you say whether it was before, after, or during the time of the death of the bodies that you found in that warehouse.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, no. All I can say is that a fire took place there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Yes, please. If we could have P2591, and if we could go first to page 23 in e-court. And this is appendix 2, I think, of the report coming up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Hedley, can you tell us -- you mentioned briefly a computer-generated image which wasn't on the screen when you spoke about that. But can you tell us what was shown in this part of your report, which we see covers the frontage of the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's the north aspect of the warehouse as we discovered it in September 2000. I think that photograph must have been taken in October 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And perhaps we should scroll down so we can see also the second image. If we can try to have both as best possible on the screen at the same time, and if you can explain what are the differences?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: As I said, we went back to the warehouse to look at the baseline of where we suspected the original doorway was, and we found quite definite witness marks on the ground. When I say "witness marks," there has been a compression of the open box girders pressing on the ground for a period of time which should -- created either a rust stain or a compression in the soil or the surface which remained once the -- once the frame itself had been removed. So from that we could ascertain the width of the doorway, and from the recovered open box girders from Glogova 1 site, we could ascertain the height of the doorway. From that, the measurements of the fixed prefabricated slabs that slotted into the wall construction, allowed us to precisely place the original doorway, show the dimensions of the original doorway, but also show the missing fins, one of the fins that had been demolished during the gaining of access or increasing slightly the size of the aperture of the doorway to get that digger in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And I know you have now mentioned a couple of times, and given a clarification of the meaning of "witness marks," but if I may I would like to paraphrase what I understand and make sure this is going to be correct on the record. You are saying that there were marks that you were able to identify on the ground at the site of the doorway which allowed you to establish the size of the original doorway even though that was no longer in place when you visited the warehouse. Have I got it roughly right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: That's a good summary, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And if we could go on to the next page in the report, please. This is a chart which -- perhaps we could zoom in just towards the top so we can see some of what's on the screen. This is a chart, as far as I can see, of items listed by grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us what this chart is cataloguing? What does it show us?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: Well, a scenes of crime officer in a domestic situation would, let's say, collect the exhibit, list the exhibits, and suggest to the investigating officer a way forward in comparison of the control samples against the samples found elsewhere. So as you see in the chart that I've prepared here, in black I have listed the samples; in red I have suggested the comparison, the forensic comparison or the investigative comparisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: So is it correct that your investigation involved collecting control samples of materials present at the Kravica warehouse and in one instance also the tiles from one of the destroyed houses in Glogova, and then you would compare materials found in the Glogova graves to see whether they matched those samples?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: That's correct. Such was the nature of the control samples taken and the scientific comparison, that would have to be made -- that would have to be made by forensic scientists of the particular skill required. In respect of the girder that was found in Glogova, one in the grave, one within the spoil, we were able to compare the two girders at a right angle, and because there was evidence of a broken weld, placing the broken weld next to each other, it was obvious to either scientist, it was obvious to the naked eye that those two welds formed a perfect visible fit. Those were obviously photographed in that position with a scale next to which, should they need to be submitted, that would be on view for confirmation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask if a packet of photographs that is currently marked as 65 ter 7524, provisionally, could be added to our 65 ter list. These are photographs from the investigation that Mr. Hedley carried out. They have only just been disclosed to the Defence. I believe a set of around 50 photos was given to the Defence on CD, I've also provided hard copies of around a dozen images to the Defence before Court this afternoon, and I understand that there isn't an objection to their addition if Your Honours would agree to that. They are -- involve showing objects that were found both at the warehouse and in the graves, and in some cases are marked with identifying numbers that are mentioned in the expert report itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your request is only related to the 13 photographs listed in this -- in your Defence list of exhibits; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: In the Prosecution list of exhibits. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. You don't have a Defence list. Sorry, yes. You are right. The reason is that in your list you used the term "Defence list of potential exhibits," and I took this -- or perhaps I -- no, this is indeed your list and the heading is --

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the two lists today are identical, in fact. I think the Defence have copied our list for their proposed exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Oh, now I realise what happened here. It looked so similar. Thank you very much for this clarification. Mr. Tolimir, Mr. Gajic, is there any objection to add these photographs to the 65 ter exhibit list?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have no objection, but the list of our exhibits is identical with the Prosecution schedule in keeping with the instructions of the Trial Chamber that whatever we intend to use we must put on the schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Leave is granted to add these photographs to the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. And if we could have that exhibit up -- or that 65 ter document up on the screen, it's 7524. And if I may, I would ask that we could start at page 3. It would make more sense in the sequence if I do it this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Now, sir, we have already seen a few images now of the doorway at Kravica. Just for some background, before we look at some more images closer up, does this look the way the doorway was when you were visiting the crime scene in 2000?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2 now, please. And in fact, if we could zoom in to the centre where you can see a small white label on the metal lattice there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you tell us what we can see here both in terms of the material in the picture but also the labeling which I note states GL01 053A.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: I am just checking on my proposed comparison list for that particular artefact number. I am afraid that doesn't help me at all, and it appears to be a place where I might have taken a control sample from; otherwise, I can't see the significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Were GL numbers ever used -- But first of all, what does a GL number signify?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, right. That's -- when we first visited the site, Kravica KA01 was not designated, so we collected control samples but entered them into the Glogova 1 log. They were stored within the log but stored separately within the artefact box. When authority was received from the investigating team to designate Kravica as a crime scene, it was then it was given the KA01 designation. At that point we transferred the control samples from the Glogova 1 log into the Kravica log. So what you see in there is a Glogova artefact number which subsequently became a Kravica artefact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And could we now zoom out from that image to see the whole of that picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Looking at that, does that give you any better idea of what we are seeing and what kind of materials are visible in the image?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: Well, we have got concrete with reinforcing bars going through it. There is a wire mesh gate above it. I don't recognise -- can't describe what the silver item is. It could have been -- it could well have been a hinge mechanism.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And if we could go back to page 3 in e-court again, just see whether we can place that image, the one we are just looking at now, the one we see --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's quite clear now. The metal strip on the left-hand side of the doorway did, in fact, form a make-shift hinge for the mesh door which, incidentally didn't have any damage to it in terms of bullet holes or any blast marks on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Okay. And I will just go through a sequence of the other photos in this packet and ask you, as each one comes up, to comment, if you can, on what we see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: So can we go to page 1 on e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a piece of concrete recovered from one of the graves. I think I describe it in the report as being 700 millimetres square. As you can see there's bullet damage to the front of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And could we go to page 4 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we saw that previously in Jean-Rene's photograph. It shows the girder removed from, I think, grave G, but I must double-check on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And just to be clear about the difference in terminology between you and Professor Wright, is this what you would call an open-box girder and he would call a rolled seal joist?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: That's correct. We are talking about one and the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And if we could see page 8 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's -- we went through the process of putting it through the two, the upright and the horizontal together at the welded point to show the physical fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And where were these items found?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: One of the girders was found in grave G, the other girder was found in the spoil, initially, when the surface of the grave was taken off.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And were you able to establish where they've come from?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: We're pretty certain by the dimensions of the open box section that they originally formed the doorway of the Kravica warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could we have page 9, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's not a particularly good photograph that, because it's pretty well shaded. But you can see the -- I mean, I can't make it out there, but -- is there a better photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I believe there is a photo of one part of this. We can look at page 7, although it doesn't show the angle of the join.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see, yes. You can see the weld mark up on the left of the bracket.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Is this the item you were talking about when you described a weld that could be seen to match?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: I am afraid the photograph isn't as clear as I recall it. We took some quite definite shots which were -- which showed that perfect physical fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I won't ask you to see things that aren't easy to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see it's the break and I've probably got two to three minutes left and then I will be done with these photos and also with the witness. So if you don't mind continuing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should continue and then we will have our break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Page 11, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That shows a component part of the doorway and the buckled metal. Now, this damage -- some of this damage could have been caused during the excavation, because as I say we were using a backhoe, truck with a backhoe to take out the earth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Again, where was this found, just for the record?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: Again, I would have to go back to the log. It was found at Glogova, and it refers to Glogova 368A. If you have copies of the log, that would help.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Page 12, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That shows us the collection of white painted concrete that was found within the grave. It shows one artefact number which was the policy adopted by Professor Wright because of the number of pieces that were coming up. For the purposes of mapping we had to show the spread of the finds. So I subsequently took representative samples from those particular stones for submission for comparison.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Page 13, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That shows a selection of the motor vehicle parts, and I see there were also tools which were found within the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And finally, could we see page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And we have already talked about the blue tiles, but I just want to look at one of those images.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: Yeah, that was found within the grave. The exact location would be shown under GL01 240A.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And if we go to page 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Now, here you've already read back to us part of the report where you described taking a control sample from the destroyed house and in the report you refer to GL01 266A. Does what we see here then reflect the control sample that was taken from the destroyed house?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: That would be the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask if the photo packet could be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The 13 photographs will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7524 shall be assigned Exhibit P2592. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Just to finish up with that, the blue tile story. So could you tell us then the locations where you took controls for blue tiles and where also you found evidence of blue tiles?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: Evidence of broken blue tiles was found within the graves of Glogova 1 site. The control sample for the purposes of comparison were taken from Kravica warehouse, and this particular sample was taken for elimination from one of the demolished houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions. Witness, thank you very much. And I'm sorry to keep everyone five minutes longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Elderkin. We must have our first break now and we will resume after half an hour, at 20 minutes past 4.00, and after that Mr. Tolimir is commencing his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedley, as I told you earlier, Mr. Tolimir is now conducting his cross-examination. I would kindly ask you again to speak a little bit more slowly, especially when you are mentioning names. Please, it is -- we need everything on the record, and if it's not there, then, then it doesn't exist, and that would be not very favourable. Please slow down and speak up a little bit, because the interpreters don't understand you properly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will do my best, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please, your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May God's peace reign supreme in this courtroom and may God's will be done today in these proceedings, and not necessarily mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to welcome the witness to say courtroom. I will have a few questions with regard to your report, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please call up the report in e-court. We saw it before the break, 52591 is the number. Let's look at page 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think you are referring to the -- to the report of Mr. Hedley; is that correct? This is now P2591. Try, please, to use that number. We have a quite different one on the record at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, I apologise. It is 65 ter 7519, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. And this is now P2591. But the number is -- the 65 ter number is incorrectly recorded again. It is 65 ter 7519. Mr. Tolimir, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Let us look at page 4 in the report. The title is: "Professional Experience."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I am reading the Serbian version. I suppose it will be the same in English as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just for the record this is page 3 in English in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let's look at page 3 in English and let's look at the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Where you say in lines 4 through 8: [As read] "He attended the exhumation of eight grave-sites in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, his responsibility being the identification, recording, collection, packaging, security, and continuity of custody of all the evidence recovered from each site. In all, this accounted for nearly 600 bodies and many hundreds of body parts and associated exhibits (artefacts)." My question is this: When you were in Croatia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina, does this number of over 600 bodies and body parts refer to your work in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: It includes both those -- both those states, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have data for each of the states and each of the localities where you worked? Do you have separate data for each of those?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: No, I don't have that. I'd have to confer and come back to you with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please speak up a little bit, a bit louder if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Would we find information on that in your report with regard to the site in Glogova? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: No. That was not my field of expertise in assessing numbers of individuals and body parts. That would have been in Professor Wright's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now go to page 4 in your report and let us now look at the first paragraph. The title of that page is: "Glogova 01." It's the next page in e-court, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "On the 23rd of August ...," I am reading the first paragraph. [As read] "On the 23rd of August, 2000, the ICTY forensic exhumation team commenced work to uncover the site of an alleged mass grave situated at a location identified as Glogova 01. The site was designated the site code GL01. (Map reference 61 degrees, 0.5 north and 96 degrees, 2 east). "Information has been received alleging that during July 1995, male victims, believed to lie within the grave, had been part of a group who had walked the mountain route from Potocari and Srebrenica towards Tuzla." My question is this, sir: Can you tell us when it comes to Glogova, people went missing en route from Potocari and Srebrenica towards Tuzla, were their bodies also found in this Glogova grave? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: On that page I am purely describing my understanding of the situation that I understood it to be at the time, so I can't answer that question. I have no knowledge of the history of the event in that respect.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, let us go to page 6 in this report. I am calling up page 6. The title is: "Kravica Warehouse." It is page 5 in English, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We are interested in paragraph 2 on page 5. The part in quotation marks, in italics, I am going to read. "The warehouse was identified at an early stage as an execution site of Bosnian Muslims and has been subject of several searches by ICTY investigators and a subsequent forensic examination was carried out between the 30th September and the 1st October 1996 by investigators from the United States Naval Criminal Investigations Service. Officers recovered 149 representative blood, hair, and tissue samples from the building, and subsequent analysis revealed 142 of these samples contained human DNA." My question: Was it established whether the 149 samples of human DNA which were identified from the Kravica warehouse were identical to the DNA samples from Glogova 01 site?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: I can't confirm that. The reason why that particular extract is in the report and it's an extract from Dean Manning's report, it was placed in there purely and simply to indicate that my examination was not the first examination. This was one of very many examinations, so the accused would have to refer to Dean Manning's report and any results arising from those DNA samples.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Hedley, do you know whether the subsequent analysis of the 149 samples was carried out in the United States or right there on the site or elsewhere? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: I do not know that. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hedley.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we look at page 15 -- or 16 in Serbian, which would be number 15 in English. If it's 16 in Serbian, it must be 15 in English. We are still looking at the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My legal assistant is going to help me with this. Let's see what we are looking for --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the record, this is page 12 in English in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank the Registry. I need the previous page, number 11 in e-court, both in Serbian and in English, thank you. And I apologise for not being very precise in calling up the pages in e-court. I have somewhat dated material in front of me and the page numbers do not exactly tally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On page 8 of the report, you stated that on the 7th of September, 2001, you carried out the first inspection of the areas; is that correct? I am talking about Kravica warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: That's correct. I've found the page, now. On the 7th of September I undertook the first of six visits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I am just rising for a correction. I believe General Tolimir talked about 2001. When I read the report it reads 2000. Perhaps we could confirm that, for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedley, you are referring to which year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 7th of September, 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And then you said on page 14 -- which is actually not page 14 but page 2, you say that your last visit to Kravica warehouse was on the 20th of October 2000; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of the fact that between the 7th September 2000 to 20th October 2000 you visited the location six times. Could you please tell us whether during the period of six weeks was Kravica warehouse continuously secured? Were there guards throughout all that time when you decided to carry out your inspection visits to the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: No, sir. It was not secured.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that we should refer to Mr. Wright's report because he was the team leader for forensic exhumations. Let us look at his report drafted for the year 2001. He claims in his report that 249 body parts were found in Glogova and that they were placed in a total of 32 body packs. Do you remember that that was indeed done? You said on page 3 in e-court that you were in charge of safe-keeping the evidence and artefacts exhumed from all of these graves?
