utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: I couldn't confirm those figures. No, I didn't count the bodies. They would correspond with the site log.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In that case let's please look at P873, page 3. This is Mr. Wright's report and a short summary thereof. Thank you. And while we're waiting for the document to appear, I would like to look at it together with you because you wanted us to refer to Mr. Wright's report. You said that on page 5. You mentioned his name. I am going to read his words back to you. [As read] "In September and October 2000, I supervised a team that found and exhumed a series of graves dug by heavy machinery at the site called Glogova 1, in eastern Bosnia and west of Bratunac. We exhumed 191 bodies. Severe robbing of the graves by heavy machinery, and removal of an unknown number of the original bodies, means that 191 is a minimum number. Many of the bodies show signs of blast damage; remains of exploded grenades were found with the bodies, together with rifle bullets. Several objects considered to be from the Kravica warehouse were found in the graves, and Mr. Michael Hedley is writing a separate report on the connection between the warehouse and Glogova 1." My question to you, sir, is this: Was the total number of bodies found at Glogova 1 indeed 191? You have just heard a summary of Mr. Wright's report on the site. So bearing that in mind, could you please answer my question? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: I am neither qualified nor had an involvement in the assessment of the bodies. This would have been done possibly by Professor Wright, most likely at the mortuary. I was purely the scene of crime officer who was handling the bodies, handling the body parts, and handling the artefacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, did you secure them, did you guard them as it says on page 3 in e-court? It says on that page, and I have just quoted the summary back to you where it says that you were in charge of guarding the material exhumed from each of those graves? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: I just say there might be an error in the translation. The fact of guarding. I never physically guarded the exhibits. I was responsible for their security in that I was provided with refrigerated containers. Each had a means of locking the containers. I was supplied with padlocks. Onsite I had an artefact box. That also had a padlock when we left it unattended. When a body was recovered from the grave or body parts were recovered from the grave in any number, we would carry those down to the locked refrigerated container. We would open the container, we would put the body parts or bodies in the container. And then we would relock it. We would walk back to our SOCO station and then resume our duties. At the end of the day, or perhaps more than once a day, we would take the recovered artefacts, we would carry them down to the secure container, unlock the container, place the items in there, lock it, and then return to our duties. At the end of the day we ensured that that the containers were locked. We had a permanent presence on-site of UN security officers, and I was satisfied that the recovered bodies, body parts, and artefacts were secure whilst in my possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since Professor Wright said 191 bodies were found, exhumed, is there a possibility that more bodies were exhumed at that location or just the number quoted by Professor Wright who is in charge of the exhumations and the analysis for Glogova 1 and Glogova 2?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: I am just not qualified to answer that question. I have not go knowledge of a minimum number of individuals of combing more bodies or whatever. We were purely -- as scenes of crime officers we were told there was a body or we were told it was a body part, and we logged it accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the report P170, page 12 in English, Mr. Janc said that 224 persons were identified in Glogova 1 and 169 in Glogova 2 which in total is 393. My question is: In view of the data presented by Mr. Wright and Mr. Janc, how do you explain this difference between 191 and 393 in localities of Glogova 1 and Glogova 2?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: I can't explain it at all. As I say the designation of B, body, or BP, body part, was given to me by an anthropologist or an archeologist or, in fact, Professor Wright on site. And that was how it was recorded. I don't know whether they were re-recorded in the mortuary when they were found, perhaps, to be a body, or there might have been less elements present, so redesignated as a body part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hedley, can you tell us who had supervision over the bodies and body parts?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: Supervision. Once they were removed from the grave I had supervision of the body bags which contained bodies or body parts. They were assigned B or a BP number. They were stored within the container, the refrigerated container on the site. There was never a discrepancy on our log sheet to that which we handed over to the mortuary at the end of a particular period. So yes, I had security. I never lost anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hedley. Does that mean that when Mr. Wright who said there were 190 bodies, there is a discrepancy with the number that you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises. Mr. Tolimir needs to repeat his question. It was not understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the interpreters didn't understand your question. Please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Hedley, was there a comparison between the number of bodies and body parts that you found and the number presented by Professor Wright who said that there were only 191; whereas, some more body parts were found? Were they found to be identical and is there an explanation for any discrepancy?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: All of the information Professor Wright would be basing his figures on, I would suspect, came from the log sheets which we kept. So comparing Professor Wright's figures, the log sheet would, I assume, give him that number. I didn't physically count them. I didn't keep a tally of how many bodies, how many body parts, and how many artefacts. I purely and simply recorded them and ensured their safe custody. I didn't take anything away or add anything to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hedley. I am not blaming you for that. I am just asking if the figures of Mr. Wright were identical to yours for Glogova 1 and 2 at the time of exhumations and at the time when you were in charge of safe-keeping?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: I will have to ask Mr. Tolimir to repeat that question. I didn't quite understand. May I read it off the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You can see the summary on the screen. In line 4, you see, "We exhumed 191 bodies." Can you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. On which screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: On the screen with the document with the heading: "Summary Findings."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, this is Professor Wright's figures, and you quoted from Mr. Janc's figures. I am not familiar with either of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's leave Mr. Janc aside. I am asking you to tell the Trial Chamber, is it possible that the number of bodies recorded by Professor Wright in his final analysis is identical to the number of bodies you safe-guarded at localities of Glogova 1 and Glogova 2?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: I would have to carry out an audit of the log sheet and compare the number of Bs in the B column and see whether we had 191 Bs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I was asking only about Glogova 1, actually. Not Glogova 2. I am asking you again: Is it possible that there are discrepancies in numbers because Professor Wright quotes the figure of 191 bodies found at Glogova 1. Is it possible that more bodies or fewer bodies were found?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: I don't think so. We logged each body, each body part, and each artefact that came out of the grave at Glogova 1. If I was told by the exhuming anthropologist or archeologist it was a body, I was assign it a "B" suffix. So therefore any count of the bodies coming from Glogova 1, it would a count of the Bs within the columns, the columns of the designated numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hedley. Let's go to another issue. Professor Wright said 191 bodies were exhumed at Glogova 1; whereas, Mr. Janc, in his report, said 224 bodies were exhumed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, before you move to another issue, Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I just want to clear my understanding. Is it your testimony that you received the body parts or the bodies and artefacts from an archeologist or an anthropologist, you logged it in; and subsequently, Professor Wright used your log sheet to compare his own report with regard to these 191.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would assume that. He would certainly have a copy of the whole of the logs from which he would extract his information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: So it is okay to say your -- it is okay to say his figures and yours should tally.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They should tally, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Okay, thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness Mr. Hedley. You have talked about the total number of bodies and body parts with which you worked and that was 600. And here you are telling us that you are not qualified to determine whether something is a body or a body part and it is Professor Wright who is qualified to talk about that or perhaps another anthropologist or archeologist. Now, concerning your work in Croatia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina that involved 600 bodies and body parts, this number, 600, who gave it to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That either came from my scenes of crime manager at the mortuary or, perhaps, Dean Manning. And it was just an indication in my preamble of my experience as to how much experience I had to give you an indication attaching to my CV. I didn't personally identify each one as a body. It was purely and simply from the records which were available to the people -- the persons I asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Then - and now please correct me if I'm wrong, because I want to understand this, what you're work involved. Your report had the purpose of establishing a link between mass graves, notably Kravica -- or, sorry, the mass graves of Glogova 1 and 2, and the Kravica warehouse. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The purpose of the report was to show a connection between Kravica warehouse and Glogova 1, not Glogova 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you. And that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Hedley, was Mr. Manning also in Croatia because this number of 600 bodies and body parts is a number that you presented for the whole theatre of war in Bosnia and Herzegovina as well as Croatia. Was Mr. Manning in Croatia as well?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: No, sir. He was part of the Srebrenica team, but he could have given me part of the -- if, in fact, it was Dean Manning, he could have given me part of the figure. It could have been given by my SOCO supervisor from the mortuary who could have given me the other part of the figure who was in both Croatia and, of course, involved in the Srebrenica post-mortems.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at P170, page 12 in English. That's the report of Mr. Janc where he said that Glogova 1 identified 224 persons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't answer that. I have never read Mr. Janc's report. I don't know what he's basing his figures on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Look, please, at this table, where he says -- the first table, where he says Glogova 1, 224 bodies identified. My question to you is, is it an increase in the number of 31 over Professor Wright's figure of 191?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: But you use the word "identified," was that the identity of the victims? Because identity of a victim could come from a body part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. He identified individuals, 224 individuals, that means those are bodies, not body parts; whereas, Professor Wright said 191 bodies were exhumed. He never spoke about body parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: General Tolimir should please refer to the part in Dusan Janc's report where he's saying that these are identifications bodies and not body parts. My understanding of Dusan Janc's report is that he is talking about DNA identifications and does not specify whether DNA extraction comes specifically from bodies only or also comes from body parts as Mr. Hedley rightly indicated is possible. So if there is that reference, I'd like to hear it. If it's not there, then please could the question be rephrased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Elderkin. I will rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Hedley, you see this report, this table, where Mr. Janc says 224 individuals. My question is, can you tell us how come that he quotes more individuals in Glogova 1 than Professor Wright who was in charge of exhumations?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: I read the paragraph above, and it says: "DNA examinations by ICMP of human remains located within the Glogova 1 grave indicate the following numbers of Srebrenica victims." So I assume that they found 224 individuals as a result of DNA testing, but I would suspect that the discrepancy is come from the testing of body parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hedley. But tell us, the people who are doing the analysis, other than pathologists and experts, are they allowed to increase the total number presented by Professor Wright who said there were 191 individuals identified? That he exhumed 191 bodies.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: That's totally beyond the realm of my experience and knowledge. I just can't answer the question. If Professor Wright has mentioned the figure 191, I would assume he took it off the Glogova 1 evidence log. What happened subsequently, I really can't answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hedley, on 28 April this year, Witness PW-064 testified here, page 15439, lines 16 to 23. And he said investigation showed that there were -- the investigation of the OTP revealed that there were 1.301 bodies buried in the Glogova mass grave. Are you surprised by this figure? My question is: Does this huge number, 1.301 as opposed to 191, show that the OTP investigation considerably increased this number, and is the Prosecution allowed to do this with the figures produced by experts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I don't recall this specific evidence of another witness. You should indicate if you are referring -- if this witness was referring to Glogova 1 or Glogova 2 or even to other mass grave-sites. To compare these figures without a clear indication to which grave-site these numbers refer, it is not a fair way to do that. I think we need some more information.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You see this page on the screen, Glogova 2, 169 individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now you are --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Sorry, 169 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now you are referring again to the report of Mr. Janc. The present witness, Mr. Hedley, said he never read this report. It's quite difficult for him to comment on these numbers, but just a minute ago you were referring to the evidence of another witness, a protected witness. You should give us the opportunity to look at the transcript at the relevant page or you should indicate if you are referring to Glogova 1 or Glogova 2 or both or to whatever a mass grave. But if we have that on the screen, we should not broadcast that part of the transcript. Perhaps the Court can produce it and put it on the screen. But, Mr. Tolimir, you reviewed the transcript, you should be in the position to give us a clear indication what you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I read from page 13439, lines 16 through 23, testimony from 28 April, 2011, protected witness 064. I can tell you the name if you wish, but we would need to move into private session, although I don't think it's really necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If it is not broadcast, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I was reading out the question by the Prosecutor to this witness, and I would now like to go back to the previous document, the report of Mr. Janc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, we want to have the opportunity to look at the transcript. Where can we find these figures? Mr. Tolimir, please point that out.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This is the right page, and the lines 16 through 23 are now marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the question of the Prosecutor was related to this Glogova grave-site. I don't know which grave-site this was. And then the answer is, I quote: "It's probably a credible figure because there was work at the location for five or six days. I was there for only limited periods of time, and if my assumption is that between 4- and 500 people were buried there when I was there, then the total you presented may well be a credible number." So this is what we can take from the transcript. But there is only a reference to a Glogova grave-site, and therefore the question remains open if this is a reference to Glogova 1, Glogova 2, or even other grave-sites. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Hedley, were only at Glogova 1?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, that was the only grave I attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at P170, page 12 in English, the report of Mr. Janc. He, as an OTP investigator, deals with both grave-sites, Glogova 1 and Glogova 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And the total he mentions is 393 individuals, identified from both localities, Glogova 1 and Glogova 2. At Glogova 1, 242; and at Glogova 2, 169; which is in total 393. How can that suddenly turn into 1.131, which is the figure found by the OTP as opposed to the figure produced by anthropologists and archeologists?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: I can't answer the question. I am not qualified. I am not familiar with the figures. I am not the right person to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is not the first time the witness is giving this answer because it was not in the limits of his duties over there, as we all know. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I am just trying to get his views with regard to the report that was published on behalf of the witness. I did not subtract anything. I didn't add anything, and I'm just quoting the Prosecutor's findings from a locality that this witness investigated and analysed, and there is a huge discrepancy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't want to discuss the matter with you. Please carry on and put the next question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Let us now look at annex 3 to your report. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to correct the figure on page 57, line 2 [sic], the report said not "242 individuals identified from Glogova 1," but in the report it was "224." Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I previously called up annex 3. This is an overview of the area and graves at Glogova 01, but I don't have that on the screen. Thank you. Now I have it. It's page 24 in English, thank you. Can we have both pages and can they be zoomed in for the benefit of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the meantime, I would like to make another correction. I didn't say "page 57, line 2," but "57, line 13" of today's transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Sir, what we have here is a table referring to Glogova 01, Kravica warehouse. This is where you represented area A, area B, grave C, grave E, grave F, grave H, grave K, grave L. These are just the totals from this table. My question to you, sir, is this: In his report, was Mr. Wright in charge of all of those graves and is the number of 191 bodies the total number of bodies exhumed from all the graves, and where -- did you attend all of the graves that you mention in your report? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: We were on call for each one of those graves. They obviously all didn't come together. They were uncovered one at a time. And we would receive from those graves bodies, body parts, and artefacts, which we dealt with in the way I previously described.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, my question was this: In graves C, E, F, H, and K, were the 191 bodies described by Dr. Wright in his analysis and in the summary that we read out before the break, were the 191 bodies exhumed from those graves that are referred to in your report?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: Again, it -- Professor Wright would report upon the bodies, the locations, and the designation. I purely received them after they had been designated. I never changed the designation. They remained as they were given to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hedley, for all of the answers you have provided. Thank you for coming to testify here today. I don't have any more questions for you. I wish you a safe journey back home. God bless you in your future work and life.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence has no further questions of the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Elderkin, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If I may just on one topic, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: This concerns the questions that we heard, including, for example, at page 57, lines 11 to 15, when General Tolimir asked about the numbers of Glogova-related victims and how it was possible that the number could be as high as 1.131.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Hedley, do you know if any Srebrenica-related graves were disturbed such that human remains were moved to other graves before ICTY investigations began?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL HEDLEY
utterances.text: I am not sure. I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: That's all I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedley, you will be pleased that this concludes your examination here in this trial. Thank you very much that you were able to come to The Hague and to provide us with your expertise and your recollection. You are now free to return to your normal activities. Thank you very much again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, Ms. Hasan is leading the next witness. If I may be excused and I can also then make sure that people are heading into the courtroom to replace me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, indeed. Have a good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In that case, to save some time, we should have our second break now and resume at 6.00 and then start with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness should be brought in, please. And welcome to you, Ms. Hasan, back to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to the Defence and to everyone else in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to confess that my question at the beginning of today's hearing about the length of cross-examination was only because of my personal mistake. I didn't want to blame anybody, not the Defence, not the Registry, not the staff of the Chamber. I just had forgotten and was confused by another matter. I wanted to put that on the record so that nobody has the feeling I would like to blame somebody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please stand a moment. Good afternoon, sir. Welcome to the courtroom. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, please, sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And make yourself comfortable. Ms. Hasan has questions for you. She is conducting the examination-in-chief. Ms. Hasan, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, witness.

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could you pleases state your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: My name is Jan de Koeijer.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: My profession is -- I am at the moment team leader of -- I'm a forensic expert in document examination, but at the moment I am team leader of a group that does interdisciplinary forensic research, but I have been a document examiner for the past 20 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could page 62, line 4, please be corrected. We have now another witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, 19 years, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, that was not in relation to you, but we have a wrong name on the transcript. And could you please repeat the name because your answer in relation to your name was not properly recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: As well. That was page 62, line 8.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Johan de Koeijer. No, it's not Johan. J-a-n de Koeijer. De Koeijer is correct in the transcript. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would kindly ask the court reporter to correct line 4 of page 62. Ms. Hasan, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Let's start with your formal education. Do you have any degrees?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: I've a degree in chemistry.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And at what level is that?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Masters degree.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Where did you obtain that degree from?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: I obtained that degree in the University of Utrecht here in the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: What year did you obtain your degree?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: I have to just check my resume. I'm sorry. I obtained my degree in 1988.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. De Koeijer, I noticed that you are looking through some papers that in front of you. Could you please just tell us what's in that file that's before you?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Well, the papers I am just looking through is my resume, which I have a Dutch and an English version, and the rest is the case file which I have with me with the report and other matters dealing with the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: In terms of forensic document analysis, have you received any training in that field?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Yes, I received a training of about four years before I did my examination and became an expert, and this training was in-house training at the Netherlands Forensic Institute.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit more about what that training comprised of?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: The training is training under a mentor, it's on the job training, partially, so doing case work under supervision. It also deals with taking courses in specifics like courses in law, courses in statistics, courses in reporting, so we have a whole number of courses which are the general courses each examiner must undergo, then we have specific literature training, studying the literature dealing with document examination and related topics.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down and please make pauses between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is a request for both speakers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Are forensic document examiners, do they typically receive a license or do they receive any certification of any form?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: At the Netherlands Forensic Institute we have a certification programme where after -- well, two to four years of training, depending on other activities, we undergo an exam, and this exam is with an external expert present and another -- and other people on the examination committee from within the institute. This certification is repeated every four years.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And when you say that certification is repeated, what does that entail?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: That entails that a similar committee is assembled every four years, usually each time with a different external expert, and we go through the same routine looking through case work. Usually we put in four to six case reports and they are reviewed by the external expert and questions are asked, and also it is looked into your resume to see if you kept up with your training and kept up with international contacts and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And who else sits on this examination board?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: We have besides the external expert, a principal scientist from our institute, the head of the department, a person from our personnel team, and a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: When did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, when you did you receive your personal certification?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: I received my personal certification in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Are you a member of any professional bodies that are relevant to the field of forensic document analysis?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Yes, I am a member of a number of bodies. One body here in the Netherlands which is called Quality Circle on Documents and -- I just have to see the translation. I'm sorry. I am not used to doing this in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I believe --

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Yeah, it's the Quality Circle on Documents, with members -- all document examiners in Holland are a member of this. I am also a member of the American Academy of Forensic Science, of the document section there, and a member of the American Society of Question Document Examiners.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And I take it these are the professional bodies that you've listed on page 1 of the English version of your --

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: -- CV?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And I see from your CV that you were on the steering committee of the European Document Experts' Working Group?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us just what projects that steering committee --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please pause between question and answer and the next question. We have some problems.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This steering committee -- this working group does work on harmonisation of methods and techniques within the document community, so we have done a lot of writing of methods relevant to document examiners. Furthermore, we are combining areas of research in documents, and we are organising conferences to help exchange knowledge between document examiners within Europe.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Have you authored any articles on these topics or on forensic documents examination generally?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Yes, I have authored a number of articles on document examination. Some on the more chemical aspects of ink analysis, and some also on some physical examinations of ink and toner.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And these articles that you've authored, have they been published in peer-review journals?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Yes, all articles published -- are published -- they are all published in the standard peer-review journals for forensic science. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Do you hold any teaching positions?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Yes. I teach at a number of different locations, one is the University of Amsterdam, a forensics course. The second is the Hogeschool of Amsterdam, it's a technical college of Amsterdam, they also have a forensics course. We also teach the judges and the lawyers in the Netherlands specific to document examination, and I also teach an international course on document examination given to mainly border control police and people from other forensic labs which come to Holland for this course.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And in terms of the subject matter of the field itself, what types of services do forensic examiners provide?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: What type of service? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: In terms of what are the general tasks of domestics -- sorry, a forensic examiner would be tasked to do?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: At the NFI, we have two major types of cases, one is an analysis of anonymous or threatening letters to determine the origin thereof; and the second part is more general document examination, it could be contracts, it could be bank documents, it could be fire-damaged documents, water-damaged documents, all kinds of documents which are in the -- which come to us from the police or from the prosecutor dealing with criminal trials.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And what sort of things are you looking for?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Well, we look for, for example, for authenticity of a document to try and see if the document has undergone changes, and we will sometimes need to determine if two documents come from the same source, to see if, for example, a print is made by a specific printer. We can also, like, in this case, if we have latent impressions or latent text or whatever to try and enhance that and determine what was the original entries. So it's quite broad aspect. Ink analysis is sometimes done to compare an ink to a pen from a suspect, paper analysis. All kinds of different techniques.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And have you been trained in all these aspects of the discipline that you have just described?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Yes, we have. That's partly the on-the-job training and partly the chemistry background which I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Where you are currently employed?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: I am currently employed at the Netherlands Forensic Institute.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And what is your current position?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Team leader of the interdisciplinary forensic science group.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Is this an accredited institution?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Yes, the NFI has been accredited since 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Since when have you been employed with NFI?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And just to be clear, is NFI a governmental agency, or is it a private enterprise?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: It's a governmental agency.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Does it belong to any particular ministry?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Yes, the Ministry of Justice and Security.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And generally, during the course of your work with NFI you have described the types of work that document examiners received, but with your work with NFI, who is it that assigns you work?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Work is assigned by -- well, we get the request from either the police, the prosecutor, or sometimes investigative judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And can you describe your current responsibilities as head of the interdisciplinary forensic science group?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: My current responsibilities are the group -- the group I run now is a group which deals with the larger cases which come into the institute. There is the larger murder cases, for example, where a lot of different requests are put into the institute within one case, and my section co-ordinates these larger cases and sends out a co-ordinated report on all the examinations done within the NFI.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, do you recall when you received a request from the OTP for which you're here to testify about?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Well, I don't recall it very specifically. It was to --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: The year?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Oh, the request to testify?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: No, sorry, I mean the request for you to produce a report, an expert report?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: The year?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: The year, well, it was in 1999. So my recollection of the request itself was not so -- is not so vivid in my mind, but it was the first -- I think it was the first case we did for the Tribunal so that was -- well, in that -- in that effect it was memorable.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And at the time that you received this request, what position did you hold at NFI?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: At that time I was senior forensic document examiner and also, I believe, the head of the department for document and photography.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could you briefly describe your practice at that time in 1999?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: At that time we had two document examiners, I think, myself and my colleague, and -- well, the practice was mainly doing daily case work and some research in documents. And -- well, some leadership issues but it was mainly case-work driven.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And how many cases would you say your section was involved in on a yearly basis?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: On a yearly basis we do between 100 and 200 cases. It used to be a bit more, but it's going down at the moment, but so roughly between those figures.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And after you were a senior forensic document examiner, well, at the time in 1999, did your position change at any point thereafter?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: My position's changed quite a bit. In -- we have had reorganisations within our institute. I have been head of the department of document examination, finger-prints, and photography, and then I was head of the document examination and photography, because finger-prints went separately. Then there was a period when I was only senior document examiner and someone else was head of that department. And the past two years I have been head of the department of documents and handwriting -- or team leader of that department. And, well, now, I have just switched to team leader of the new department.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. And if we can go back to 1999 when you were the head of the document section. Were you, yourself, directly involved in the examination of documents?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Did you have any supervisory role?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Also, yes. I had a trainee at that time, and I also had a role to supervise the work coming out of the photography department.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Of the cases that you worked on in your section, you know, how many of them, roughly, were for criminal cases?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: That would be more than 90 per cent because the times that we have a noncriminal case is very limited, so it would probably be 95 to 99 per cent criminal case work.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Have you ever been called to testify as an expert in the past?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: I have been called once here at the Yugoslav Tribunal, and two or three times in Dutch court.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Do you recall in which case and what you were tasked to do for this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: I was -- I know I had a -- numerous documents I had established for stamps to see if there are any alterations in the document, but I don't recall exactly for what -- who the suspect was in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this stage I would offer Mr. De Koeijer's CV into evidence. It has 65 ter number 7521 and this wasn't previously on our 65 ter list as we just recently received an updated version of Mr. De Koeijer's CV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it from my experience with the Defence that there is no objection, especially not with this document, so leave is granted to add it to the 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And I would in that case offer it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter document 7521 shall be assigned Exhibit P2593. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I am going to now turn -- just divert our attention a little bit to the examination of documents, specifically. Could you describe the methods that experts in your field use to examine documents that have been altered?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Yes. The main methods are optical methods to look at altered documents. Microscopy is a method you usually start off with, looking at the document through a microscope. Of course, well, first you examine the document with the naked eye, but the microscope is the method which you use quite often. We will use luminescence and reflectance techniques so they are light-driven techniques where we have different types of light sources which you then look at the document with and these are mainly used to detect remnants in the document from original entries, for example. Sometimes these -- there are remnants in the document from inks which have specific properties under these different lighting conditions which make them light up or be enhanced. Other -- there are other more sophisticated chemical techniques, scanning techniques which we will seldom use. There is also -- lately we are also using more digital image enhancement techniques where we have a very good scanner to scan the document and then do image analysis. This was something which we did not do back in 1999 because, well, the scanners were not of as good quality as they are now.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 642 displayed on the screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise this as something come -- well, it's a translation, of course, but it looks like something coming from our case file system, our case system.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could we just turn to page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And what would this be?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: I recognise this as a translation of my report, the front page of my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we could just turn to page 5 now, the last page.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, do you recognise this as being -- would this have been the report that you prepared --

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: -- for the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Or the translation thereof.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And what language was the original in?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: In Dutch.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could we go back to page 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: At the very top of this page next to the word "co-ordinator," it has the letters -- the abbreviation "DO," and next to that that's been translated as "investigation director," which is followed by your name. What does the abbreviation "DO" in Dutch mean?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: The abbreviation stands for document onderzoeker which means document examiner. It's more the section within the institute where the case needs to go to or where I belong to. That's the section which I belong to.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us what -- okay, where this request originated from? Who did you receive the request from?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: The request came from the -- from ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And when you received the request, what were you asked to do?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: We were asked to examine the documents listed here to look for erased writings, examine the tables, and more specifically later on we were asked to emphasize on the specific letter "O" in the documents, where the letter O had been erased.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay, and when you say this was emphasized, what do you mean be that?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: This was in -- well, we talked to the requestee Bertel [phoen] and to limit the amount of research on the document he -- he or she, I am not sure if it was a lady or a man, specified that we should put emphasis on the letter "O" and on the legenda [sic] part of one of the pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. So do I understand you correctly that that is what you were meant to look for?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And were you provided with any materials?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Yes. We obtained four sheets with -- containing the tables. And these -- the sheet is listed at the bottom of this page.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Were these -- was this an original document?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: This is an original document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: May we have P1754 displayed. And if I may ask for the assistance of the Court Usher to hand the document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The original document or --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, the Court Usher will assist.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I think it's sufficient for this purpose to not have the English translation up for the time being, just simply the B/C/S so we can see it clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, if you could just flip through that and let us know if that is the document that you received?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Yes, this is the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And would that be the document -- did you -- sorry, did you examine the original document or would you have examined a copy of it?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: No, we examined the original document.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would offer the original to Your Honours to have a look at while the witness testifies, if you wish to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If he doesn't need it during the answers he is providing to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think I have copies with me, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's fine, the Chamber would like to see it, but also the Defence should have the opportunity to have a look. Ms. Hasan, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. De Koeijer, aside from that document, were you provided with any other materials?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Did you examine that document yourself?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Did anyone else examine the document?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: A colleague of mine examined the document first, and I examined it after him.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Is that standard procedure?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: This is -- all case work at the NFI is done by, at least within the document section, is always done by two people, and specifically if there is an interpretation issue then the second examiner will always look at the items in detail or so and do their own examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could you describe for us the techniques you used to examine this particular document?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: This particular document was examined with different types of lighting. Looking at it with transparent lighting, with oblique lighting, which is lighting from a low angle, this in combination with stereo-microscopy, we also looked at it with infrared, infrared reflectance method, which is using infrared light shining on the document and looking at the reflectance and the absorbance of the inks on the paper under this infrared light using a camera to register this. This technique is mainly done because pencil contains carbon and carbon absorbs infrared light very strongly. So if there are very weak pencil marking, they could be enhanced a bit by looking at it with infrared reflectance technique. Other technique which we tried which we did -- another technique which we tried, which we did not report, is electrostatic detection apparatus, which is a technique which looks mainly at indented writing impressions, and, well, this technique didn't work as well as the other techniques which we did report.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And can you just elaborate a little bit on what it is that this transparent or oblique lighting shows you?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: If you use oblique lighting, then impressions will show a darker rim around the impression, so they will stand out more in the paper than -- than they would with normal reflective lighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And what is a stereo-microscope?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: A stereo-microscope is a microscope which has a binocular, so you can view it with both eyes. Not just one eye, it has a binocular.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And do all these techniques or equipment, do they assist you in also discerning the underlying text?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: In addition to determining whether there has been an erasure?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If I could have the report back on the screen, which are 65 ter 6 -- no, 65 ter 642.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, on page 77, line 15, there is something that seems completely unclear to me. It says: "So you can view it with Bozovic implies." It must be an error. This sentence is completely nonsensical and in Serbian I heard something entirely different, in the interpretation, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was very clear that the witness said, "with both eyes." Please continue, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, if I may just go back to the infrared reflection technique you talked about. Now, you said you could observe -- you could use it to look at the absorption of the light when looking at documents that have ink and pencil on them. In this particular document, what is used? Is it ink? Is it pencil? What's used on this document?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: This document was written in pencil.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 3 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Under the subheading "Investigation of documents," you note that the characters on this document were written, and I will quote the English, "With considerable pressure leaving deep imprints in the paper." How are you able to see these imprints?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: These imprints you can see quite clearly with the oblique lighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Were you able to see these imprints --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please pause between question and answer at the next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Were you able to see any imprints on this document using the naked eye?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Using the naked eye you could see that part of the pencil material had not been erased fully. It's more difficult to see the imprints just with the naked eye, but you can if you're in a darkroom and use side lighting, you can then, with the naked eye. But just under normal lighting conditions, it's much more difficult. But in a darkroom with side lighting, you can with the naked eye, you can see these imprints, also, yes. You don't really -- if it's large enough, you don't need a microscope to see these imprints.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And for the entire document that you examined, did you apply all the methodologies or did you select a few for specific entries? How did you go about examining it?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: We would first examine it with the naked eye using different lighting techniques, and when you want to examine it in more detail, we would go to the microscope and examine it at a larger magnification, and that's mainly to see if there are any -- to look at the letters a bit more closely to see if there are maybe letters which may look similar. Like, if it's an "O" or it's a "C" or if the closure is correct in a -- or it may be a tail, there could have been an A, for example. That kind of detail we would look at under the microscope.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could we have the document P1754 again displayed on our screen. And could we turn to page 8. And it's sufficient if we just, I think, have the B/C/S version of the document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, based on your examination of this page, did you see -- yeah, perhaps we can centre the text a little bit more. I know it's printed that way in the original -- no, maybe not. Okay. Did you see any alteration that's been done on this page?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the witness kindly wait for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just look at the transcript and see if the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's finished, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- question is finished.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We saw below the -- or row nine, below the "T," we saw that a part of the text there -- of the text there had been erased. You see it as the white line in this legenda [sic].

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, the original document itself, do you see any evidence of erasure on that document. It doesn't --

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: It doesn't register on the copy, no. But on the document itself, you can see, very lightly, you can see it with the naked eye, but using the equipment we have we could get a better image and we are able to interpret what was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And what were you able to discern was written there before it was erased?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: The line started with the letter "O," and then there was a dash, and then the name Orahovac, O-r-a-h-o-v-a-c.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please. Is that correct, the spelling of this word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Nyambe has a question -- Ms. Hasan, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, when I met with Mr. De Koeijer earlier today he provided us with some images of this particular -- from this document that were part of his file, and these have now been uploaded onto e-court and they have the number 65 ter 7527, and I would ask leave to add these images which were recently provided to us to our witness -- to our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, do you have any objection to that request?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Leave is granted to add these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have then 65 ter 7527 displayed on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. De Koeijer, do you have those images that you gave us earlier today with you?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Again, the witness is kindly asked to wait for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how these images were captured?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: These images were captured with an apparatus called the VSC, it's a video spectral comparator. And some of the images of this image was captured with side lighting or with oblique lighting, and there are also one or two images in here which were captured with infrared reflectance.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, we will go through these images, but what I want to ask you before we get into them is do they reflect -- what we see on the screen here, is that a reflection of what you would have seen through the device you were looking through at the time?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: The image quality is always quite a bit less on printed images, and the quality is always better when viewing it directly under the microscope or with the apparatus on the screen. Once you print it, the quality is less and, well, this is of course a copy of a print of mine so the quality is, again, somewhat less. But some of the features you can see here I can also see on my copy, and some of the features I can see a little bit better maybe on my copies.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at one of the these images which is on page 4 of this document. Can you tell us what we see here on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: What we see here is a side light image, oblique light image, where we can see some of the paper -- well, the impressions in the paper. This is a pretty rough image. We have some better images for the side lighting, but you could see also the paper fibre disturbances in this image that -- also the paper has been damaged a bit, at the place of the erasure.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Let's turn to the next page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And can you tell us what we see here?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Yeah, this is also a side light image, and -- but here we see less of the paper fibre disturbances, and we see a bit more of the impressions which can be, well, deciphered partly from this image. But the image I saw on the screen and under the microscope is better than this quality, and also the one I have in front of me is somewhat better quality than this is. But here we can see the text "Orahovac."

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And let us turn to page 6 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: What are we seeing on this page?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: This is an infrared image of the same line. This image is weaker than the previous one with the side lighting, and it's -- well, it gives more or less the same information but it's more difficult to decipher.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I am going to move to some of the other findings you've made in your report which relate to your search for the letter "O." If we can look at one example.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could we go back to P1754 and turn to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to just take as an example row 1 in this table. In your examination of that row, did you find any alterations in your search or did you find any Os?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Yes, we did. In column number 14, we found that there was an original "O" entry underneath the "T."

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If perhaps we can focus in a little bit on column 14, row 1. And did you find any other alterations in this row?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Yes. In 15 -- in column 15 we found that the letter "R" had been changed to a "T."

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we're going to look at some other images of these particular findings.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we could revert back to 65 ter 7527, please. And if we could just zoom in a little bit on this page, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us what we are looking at here?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Yes, again, this image is -- the quality of this image is less than what I have in front of me, but in column 15 you can see quite well the "R" in this case, and -- but in column 14 it's still difficult to see the "O," but there are some -- well, you can see there are some round part in there around the bottom of the "T," but there is -- there should be a better image.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. And how is it that you know that this is row 1, the same row we were looking at in the other document?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Well, this is -- you can check this very easily by just overlaying this image with the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: But it's also stated on here on the image itself, which you have.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yeah, if we zoom out of this a little bit. I don't know if it's been picked up on the screen. It hasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: But in your version I note that you noted down the ERN number of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Perhaps Your Honours can take a look at the copies of the versions that he has. But for the time being, if we could then turn to the next page, I think there is another image that's been captured of these same two columns.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. De Koeijer, would you be able to answer my questions about these images without having your copies of the documents before you?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And I would just propose to hand those up to Your Honours as they are a little bit clearer than what appears on the screen, and the Defence can take a look at them as well. Well, we can just hand up the one page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is it possible for me to use a pointer of some kind?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Absolutely. The Court Usher will assist you with that in a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. This page which is now on the screen with the ERN number 0559-2134 is handed over to the Defence and to the Chamber. Please continue, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. De Koeijer, you wanted to show something using the pointer?

utterances.speaker: JAN DE KOEIJER
utterances.text: Yes. Is it just this one? In column 14 you can see the outline of the "O" here going something like this, and the "R" is -- in column 15 is like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, given that the witness has marked this particular page, I would offer this page into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This marked page will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The marked page of the 65 ter document 7527 shall be assigned Exhibit P2594. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time, and it would be a good point to end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to give the original documents we have received as the Chamber back to the Prosecution and the witness respectively. Indeed, we have to adjourn for today. Ms. Hasan will continue the examination-in-chief tomorrow and followed by Mr. Tolimir with his cross-examination. We have to adjourn and we will resume tomorrow in the afternoon, 2.15, in Courtroom III. Mr. De Koeijer, just to let you know, you have no permission to contact either party about the content of your testimony during the break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
